title: ‘Princess Diaries’ Actor Erik von Detten Accused of Elder Abuse and Fraud in Gold Scheme
description: Erik von Detten, the former Disney star known for his roles in “The Princess Diaries” and “Brink!” is facing a lawsuit alleging elder abuse and fra
body:
Erik von Detten, the former Disney star known for his roles in “The Princess Diaries” and “Brink!” is facing a lawsuit alleging elder abuse and fraud after an elderly couple claimed he persuaded them to invest more than $2 million of their retirement savings in significantly overpriced gold coins.

	The lawsuit, filed in California in May, names von Detten, 44, and his employer, precious metals company Rosland Capital, as defendants. Sheila Greenberg, 85, and her husband, Norman Greenberg, 97, allege they lost approximately $900,000 after purchasing gold coins through the company.
	

	Rosland Capital has ceased operations and declared bankruptcy in July, listing some $64 million in liabilities and just $500,000 in assets. According to filings in the bankruptcy case, the company has faced scrutiny from the New York Attorney General’s Office and the Securities and Exchange Commission.


	The creditors’ committee is seeking to subpoena Von Detten as it investigates the failure of the company, saying it appears he “played an instrumental part in the Debtor’s business and its financial collapse.”

	“The Greenbergs’ story is not unique,” the creditors’ committee alleges. “It is one of hundreds. Creditors, including the other Committee members, have described remarkably similar experiences: trust cultivated, expertise professed, reliance encouraged, and substantial savings ultimately lost with zero information about where their money has gone.”

	Rosland advertised on Fox News and Newsmax with spots starring actor William Devane, who pitched gold coins as a hedge against inflation and other sources of instability. Retirees were encouraged to convert their IRAs into gold-backed funds, and were offered “a free safe to store your gold.”
	

	According to their lawsuit, the Greenbergs contacted Rosland Capital in 2020 after seeing an ad on TV. They were connected with von Detten, who had joined the company in 2018 after largely stepping away from acting.

	The Greenbergs say they told von Detten they had limited knowledge of the gold market but approximately $2 million available in retirement savings. They allege that von Detten presented himself as an experienced adviser and encouraged them to purchase Lady Liberty gold coins as an investment.

	Von Detten did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

	Rosland reported $151 million in revenues in 2021. But according to the company’s first-day filing in bankruptcy court, the company suffered “excessive cash outflows” and racked up net losses of $24 million from 2022-25. The rising cost of gold also put a strain on the company’s business, as it was unable to keep up with customer demand, resulting in a months-long backlog in orders.

	“During this interval, the price of gold usually increased dramatically such that Debtor ended up paying more for the gold product than the customer paid Debtor for that product,” the company’s accountants reported. “This situation was not sustainable and the Debtor lost money rapidly.”

	Sales reps were paid 15%-35% of the profit on each order, regardless of whether that order was later refunded. When the company ceased operations, there were about 470 messages and voicemails either demanding refunds or demanding delivery of gold products, according to the first-day motion.

	The creditors’ committee, however, does not appear to believe that the business simply failed due to deteriorating market conditions.

	“The Committee believes the facts point to something far more troubling: a business that preyed on a vulnerable population, stole customer money while its ability to perform was collapsing, lied to its own customers about what their money would be used for, and ultimately left creditors to ask whether those funds were misused, diverted, transferred to insiders or affiliates, or simply consumed to keep the scheme alive,” the committee’s attorneys wrote.

	Von Detten was a familiar face in Disney productions throughout he late 1990s and early 2000s. He starred as the title character in the 1998 Disney original movie “Brink!” and played Josh Bryant, the love interest of Anne Hathaway’s Mia Thermopolis, in 2001’s “The Princess Diaries.”
	

	He also voiced Sid Phillips, the toy-destroying neighbor in “Toy Story” and Erwin Lawson in Disney’s animated series “Recess.” His other credits include “Escape to Witch Mountain,” “So Weird” and “Complete Savages.”

	Von Detten largely retired from acting around 2010, later transitioning into sales and financial services. He briefly reprised his role as Sid in “Toy Story 4.”

title: Costume Designer Sandy Powell to Present Film London Jarman Award – Film News in Brief
description: Oscar-winning costume designer Sandy Powell is set to present this year’s Film London Jarman Award on Nov. 24, where she will also be the guest of
body:
Oscar-winning costume designer Sandy Powell is set to present this year’s Film London Jarman Award on Nov. 24, where she will also be the guest of honor.

	Powell frequently collaborated and was mentored by Derek Jarman, whom the award was established in honor of in 2008 to celebrate U.K.-based artist-filmmakers in the film industry. Throughout her career, Powell has also worked with Martin Scorsese, Neil Jordan, Todd Haynes and Yorgos Lanthimos.
	

	“Sandy’s remarkable career speaks to a truly remarkable talent. From her days collaborating with Derek Jarman on films like ‘Caravaggio’ and ‘Edward II’ to the peerless design she has brought to a staggering array of modern classics, her work is bold, beautiful and boundlessly creative,” said Adrian Wootton, OBE, the chief executive of Film London. “She has long been vocal in her support of Derek’s cultural legacy, and, as such, I don’t think we could ask for a more fitting guest of honor for this year’s Film London Jarman Award.”


	Also working on “Cinderella,” “The Wolf of Wall Street” and “Mary Poppins Returns,” Powell received the Academy Award for Best Costume Design for “Shakespeare in Love,” “The Aviator” and “The Young Victoria.” This year’s Film London Jarman Award nominees are Sadia Pineda Hameed, Ilona Sagar, Rhea Storr and Alia Syed.
	
		Tuesday, October 20	
	
		Molly Shannon Joins “Summer 2000: The X-Cetra Story” as Executive Producer	

	Molly Shannon has joined “Summer 2000: The X-Cetra Story” as an executive producer before the film’s Los Angeles premiere at the AFI Fest on Oct. 24.

	After the screening, the Emmy-nominated actress and bestselling author will moderate a Q&A with director, writer and producer Ayden Mayeri, writer, producer and cinematographer Barry Rothbart, producer Rachael Fung and subjects Janet Kariuki, Mary Washburn, Jessica Hall and Robin O’Brien.

	“Summer 2000: The X-Cetra Story” follows a group of friends as they reunite when the album they made as pre-teens becomes a cult online hit 20 years later.

	“I was so deeply moved by this beautiful film and its reminder of how easy it is to lose track of that free-spirited, dreaming little girl inside all of us,” Shannon said. “It’s a wonderful reminder to keep making room for the things that bring us joy, no matter how much time has passed. I’m so excited to be part of this project and to help share X-Cetra’s story with audiences.”

	The film made its world premiere at SXSW and won the Documentary Feature Jury Award. Since then, it has screened at the Sydney Film Festival, Melbourne International Film Festival and the Bentonville Film Festival. After AFI Fest, it will screen at DOC NYC.

schema.headline: Costume Designer Sandy Powell to Present Film London Jarman Award – Film News in Brief

title: ‘American Horror Story’ Renewed for Season 14
description:
“American Horror Story” has been renewed for its 14th season at FX.

	The news comes ahead of the Oct. 29 finale of Season 13, which reunites franc
body:
“American Horror Story” has been renewed for its 14th season at FX.

	The news comes ahead of the Oct. 29 finale of Season 13, which reunites franchise legends Jessica Lange, Sarah Paulson, Evan Peters,  Angela Bassett, Kathy Bates, Emma Roberts, Billie Lourd, Gabourey Sidibe and Leslie Grossman.

	Other returning stars include Frances Conroy, Jamie Brewer, John Carroll Lynch, Mena Suvari and Mat Fraser, as well as Seth Gabel, who appeared in the spinoff “American Horror Stories.” Season 13 cast members who are new to the franchise include Joey Pollari, Avantika, Elle Chapman, Berto Colon, Alex Consani, Seth Gabel, Orlando Jones, Paul Anthony Kelly, Tig Notaro, Madelaine Petsch, Fedor Steer, Zach Villa, John Waters and more. Pollari plays a hospice care worker with a phobia of the number 13 who is tasked with taking care of characters from previous “American Horror Story” seasons; hence the volume of returning stars.
	

	Season 13 opened with 4 million views in four days, the best streaming performance of any premiere in the series’ history — a significant feat especially given the three-year hiatus following the 2023 premiere of Season 12, “Delicate.”


	Created by Ryan Murphy and Brad Falchuk, “American Horror Story” is FX’s longest-running hour-long series and has driven more than 2 billion hours of engagement since the launch of Season 1 in 2011. Season 13 is executive produced by Murphy, Falchuk, Ned Martel, Charlie Carver, Eric Kovtun, Nissa Diederich, Scott Robertson, Tanase Popa, Crystle Roberson Dorsey, Jennifer Salt and Tim Minear. 20th Television is the studio.

title: Keanu Reeves in Talks to Star in James Wan’s ‘The Gangster, The Cop, The Devil’ at Paramount
description:
Keanu Reeves is in talks to team with James Wan for the filmmaker’s latest project, “The Gangster, The Cop, The Devil” at Paramount Pictures. 

	Th
body:
Keanu Reeves is in talks to team with James Wan for the filmmaker’s latest project, “The Gangster, The Cop, The Devil” at Paramount Pictures. 

	The Paramount Pictures movie reimagines the 2019 Korean action-crime thriller starring Don Lee (also known as Ma Dong-seok), who is attached to reprise his role opposite Reeves. The original film — which follows a police officer and a gangster as they reluctantly join forces to track down a serial killer — debuted to rave reviews at the Cannes Film Festival that year.
	

	Wan will direct the film, his first feature since 2023’s “Aquaman and the Lost Kingdom.” He will also produce the project alongside Michael Clear and Jason Blum (via Blumhouse Atomic Monster), Lee (Big Punch Global), Sylvester Stallone and D. Matt Geller (Balboa Productions), and Chris S. Lee (B&C Group. Lorenzo di Bonaventura has also come on board to produce. The project has been in the works since 2019, with Wan boarding the production this spring. 


	Eric Pearson wrote the latest script, based on previous drafts by Shay Hatten and Brian Helgeland. Helgeland and Billy Acumen will executive produce the project.

	Reeves is an action movie icon, headlining numerous franchises from “The Matrix” movies to the “John Wick” films. He last starred in AppleTV’s dramedy “Outcome,” directed by Jonah Hill, and voiced Duke Caboom in “Toy Story 5.” He will next reprise his voice role as fan-favorite character Shadow in “Sonic the Hedgehog 4,” which Paramount has dated for March 19, 2027. Reeves is repped by WME and Ziffren Brittenham.
	

	The Hollywood Reporter first reported the actor’s involvement.

title: Netflix Q3 Revenue Meets Wall Street Estimates, Forecasts Q4 Slowdown and Says It Will Miss Ad Sales Target for the Year
description: Netflix‘s third-quarter 2026 earnings met revenue expectations and it slightly beat on the bottom line. But the streamer faces an urgent need to re
body:
Netflix‘s third-quarter 2026 earnings met revenue expectations and it slightly beat on the bottom line. But the streamer faces an urgent need to refresh its queue: Revenue growth in the period slowed to its lowest rate in three years, and the company just laid off 1,000 employees in a restructuring effort to reposition itself.

	Netflix posted Q3 revenue of $12.87 billion, up 11.8% year-over-year. That’s compared with 17% top-line growth a year ago. Net income came in at $3.66 billion (versus $2.55 billion a year earlier), translating to earnings of 87 cents per share. Operating margin was 34.6%, versus 33.2% expected.
	

	Meanwhile, the company projected Q4 revenue of $13.4 billion, which would be an increase of 11.5%. That’s below Wall Street’s prior expectations of $13.5 billion.


	For full-year 2026, the company now expects advertising revenue of about $2.7 billion, whereas it previously had been forecasting $3 billion. Netflix blamed the lower ad-revenue take on “slightly slower than expected rollout of some ad product capabilities.”

	As Netflix has seen per-subscriber engagement drift downward in recent quarters, particularly in the U.S., the company last week laid off about 1,000 employees, about 6% of its workforce. The company ousted chief content officer Bela Bajaria, tapping veteran TV exec Peter Rice to replace her, and pink-slipped head of film Dan Lin and his top lieutenant, Doug Belgrad, as well as director of original series Carolina Garcia.

	In their Q3 letter to shareholders, the Netflix management team — led by co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters — addressed the layoffs but did not explain why they decided to overhaul content leadership.
	

	Netflix currently projects a Q4 operating margin of 26.0%, which includes a 120 basis point “negative impact” for costs associated with the layoffs (but would be up compared with 24.5% in the year-ago quarter). “These organizational changes enable us to continue to aggressively invest in high impact areas to improve our service, and drive growth and innovation,” the Netflix execs said, echoing language they used in an internal company memo about the job cuts.

	For Netflix’s third quarter, Wall Street analysts on average expected $12.87 billion in revenue and earnings per share of 82 cents, per LSEG Data & Analytics.

	In July 2026, Netflix released its “What We Watched” viewing report for the first half of 2026, showing global hours viewed increased 2% year over year in aggregate — while per-user engagement has shrunk. According to estimates by analysts at Jefferies, Netflix average monthly viewing time per member globally has fallen from 66 hours in the first half of 2023 to about 49 hours in the first half of 2026.

	Netflix previously announced that it will shift to publishing the viewing report annually in the first quarter, beginning in 2027. “The goal of separating the publication of the report from our earnings results is to keep the focus on our primary financial metrics — revenue and operating profit,” the company said.

	In their Q3 letter, the execs wrote, “We know there’s some investor concern about our view hours growth. Member response to our 2026 price increases is consistent with prior price changes and our expectations, an indicator that our engagement — which encompasses quantity, quality and variety of viewing — remains healthy and that we continue to deliver strong value to members. But we do seek to accelerate growth in view hours as well, and we’re confident we’ll do that by relentlessly focusing and executing against the aforementioned strategy.”

	In 2027, Netflix plans to launch its ad-supported tier in 15 new countries in 2027. The first tranche of new market launches will happen in March 2027, spanning nine countries in Europe (Austria, Belgium, Denmark, Ireland, the Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Sweden and Switzerland), along with Colombia, Peru and New Zealand.

title: Ted Sarandos Addresses Netflix Content Exec Purge: ‘I Know That We Could Do Better’
description: Netflix, looking to boost its viewing engagement as revenue growth cools off, made a major overhaul of its executive leadership overseeing content.
body:
Netflix, looking to boost its viewing engagement as revenue growth cools off, made a major overhaul of its executive leadership overseeing content.

	Last week, amid its layoff of 1,000 employees, Netflix ousted chief content officer Bela Bajaria and has tapped veteran TV exec Peter Rice to replace her. The company also let go head of film Dan Lin and his top lieutenant, Doug Belgrad, as well as director of original series Carolina Garcia.
	

	On the streamer’s Q3 2026 earnings call, co-CEO Ted Sarandos — who had previously led Netflix’s content operations for over 20 years — explained the decision to install a new team overseeing its programming lineup led by Rice.


	“I know that we could do better, and we want to build on that momentum,” Sarandos said, when asked about the leadership change on the content side.

	Sarandos started by praising Bajaria “for all of her incredible contributions to Netflix. Bela had an incredible decade-long run here. She put a lot of great hits on the board. She led the teams through a lot of expansions of new types of content. She also did the hard work of building this incredible international team, who’s been making local content around the world, which has become a great competitive differentiator for us over the last decade.”

	That said, Sarandos continued, “Now we’ve seen an opportunity to take our slate to the next level, especially in the U.S. where we can have an outsized impact when we create a big buzzy show that members love and talk about all over the world.”

	Sarandos said he has known Rice, a former Disney and 21st Century Fox television and movie exec, for about 15 years. At Disney, he was chairman of Walt Disney Television before he was ousted by former CEO Bob Chapek in 2022.
	

	“And I’ve got to tell you the outpouring of excitement about him coming to Netflix from across the industry and from the creative community has been nothing short of overwhelming. He’s one of the really rare people in the industry who’s led TV networks, movie studios, streaming services,” Sarandos said. “His creative instinct and his business acumen are remarkable. He’s really an at-scale quality and volume operator, and he does it across every imaginable form of entertainment. You know, network [television], prestige cable, streaming, theatrical and TV films, and live sports.”

	Sarandos said, “most importantly… Peter Rice understands talent relations, and in a competitive market, creative talent have choices of where they want to work, and we want Netflix to always be the place that they love to do the best work of their life. Peter is the exact right person to lead those efforts in the U.S. and around the world. Now, that’s a key aspect of what I believe Peter can improve on looking forward.”

	A bit later in the call, Sarandos again sang Rice’s praises. 

	“Peter brings expertise in both art and commerce, television and film. It’s kind of that exact balance skill set that will help guide us through our next chapter,” Sarandos told Wall Street analysts. “Now, there’s a ton to be excited about in our Q4 slate, and a ton to be excited about in 2027. And I believe that Peter will actually be able to have an impact on those projects that are in the works, even in the short term.”

schema.headline: Ted Sarandos Addresses Netflix Content Exec Purge: ‘I Know That We Could Do Better’

title: Music Industry Moves: Barbara Cane, BMI’s VP of Worldwide Creative, to Retire After Five Decades
description: After a five-decade career with BMI, Barbara Cane has announced that she will retire from the company at the end of this year. While she is leaving
body:
After a five-decade career with BMI, Barbara Cane has announced that she will retire from the company at the end of this year. While she is leaving her current role as BMI’s Vice President of Worldwide Creative, Cane has agreed to serve in an advisory capacity to BMI, working directly with CEO Mike O’Neill.

	“After more than five decades, BMI is not simply where I have built my career — it is part of who I am,” Cane said. “It gave me the opportunity to grow, to discover, and, most importantly, to uncover the soul within the songwriter. Through every chapter of my journey, I have come to understand that creativity is not simply a profession; it is the heart of who songwriters are and the force that moves our industry forward. What has made this journey so meaningful is that my own values remain deeply aligned with those of BMI – to believe in creators, to nurture their gifts, and to create an environment in which their careers can flourish. After fifty years, that purpose still lives in my heart—and it is why this work has never felt simply like a career, but like a calling.”
	

	O’Neill added, “Barbara is one of the first people I met when I joined BMI almost 32 years ago, and her kindness, caring nature and warm welcome showed me exactly why she is so loved by so many in our industry. She has demonstrated that same care and attention time and again to the many songwriters she worked with, nurtured and supported, and it’s why her relationships in this industry have endured. While Barbara and I started out as colleagues, we’ve ended up as family, and I don’t know many who can say that about the people they work with. The beautiful thing for me is that Barbara has agreed to continue working with me as an advisor, allowing BMI and our writers to still have her insight and counsel, while also allowing her to enjoy some time away from us for the first time in fifty years.”
	

	Cane began working at BMI part-time in 1970 while she was still in high school and has dedicated her entire professional career to the company. She held numerous roles throughout her tenure, starting in BMI’s “Song Research” department and holding a number of creative roles including General Manager of the Los Angeles office as well as Vice President of Creative in New York, Los Angeles and London, directing the creative activities for BMI’s Pop, Rock and Indie teams.

	+ Electric Feel Publishing has signed songwriter and producer Naila to the company’s UK roster.

	Naila is a London-based, multilingual writer, producer and multi-instrumentalist from Barcelona who has worked with Joel Compass, H.lls, P2J, Gabzy, Moon Willis, Rimon, BenjiFlow, Mahalia, AoD, Dinos, JJ and ColeYoursTruly, among others. She has worked closely with and developed Spanish artists Violeta, Paula Cendejas, Chiara Oliver and Olivia Bay, as well as French artist Anaïs Cardot.

	“I am incredibly excited to become a part of the amazing team at Electric Feel, it’s a blessing to be surrounded by this amount of talent and skill and I cannot wait for the music and experience ahead with the EF family!” said Naila.

	+ Warner Chappell Music Nashville has struck a global publishing deal with Kentucky-reared singer-songwriter Elizabeth Nichols, known for her breakout single, “I Got a New One.” She made her Grand Ole Opry debut last November and has performed at Stagecoach, Lollapalooza, C2C and CMC festivals and has opened for Little Big Town, Jason Aldean, Russell Dickerson, and Jordan Davis.

	“I’m very excited to join Warner Chappell, where I can finally monetize my questionable taste in men. I have the best team in the world. Here’s to many more songs.”

	Katy Wolaver, SVP, A&R, Warner Chappell Music, shared: “Elizabeth is a breath of fresh air… witty, clever, and unabashed in taking authentic life experiences and turning them into irresistible lyrics and melodies. Her songs embrace a wide range of moods and emotions, from unique takes on relationships to political satire. In just a short time on the country landscape, she’s moved her career into high gear, and all of us at Warner Chappell are delighted to join her on what is sure to be an incredible ride.”
	

	+ Sony Music Publishing Nashville, in partnership with Taycan Entertainment, has signed rising songwriter and producer Jared Conrad to a worldwide publishing deal. Conrad has earned cuts with Cody Johnson, Lee Brice, Brothers Osborne, Ian Munsick, Randall King, Mitchell Tenpenny and Austin Snell, among many others. His credits also include co-writing Pentatonix and Meghan Trainor’s “Kid On Christmas” from Pentatonix’s Grammy-nominated album “Holidays Around the World.”

	+ Columbia Records has announced the expanded role of Manos Xanthogeorgis as Executive Vice President, Creative & Digital, leading a newly formed creative team while continuing to oversee digital across the labe

	In his expanded role, Xanthogeorgis will oversee creative and art direction, short- and long-form content, and the label’s digital functions, including audience development, viral marketing and social.

	“What I love about music is that something deeply personal to an artist can become just as personal to someone they’ve never met. Finding new ways to help that happen is what keeps this work so exciting for me,” said Xanthogeorgis.

title: Why ‘You Can See Everything’ Could Win Best Picture at the Oscars
description: The word disruptor is a vividly descriptive one, and it’s almost always applied to an individual. But it doesn’t have to be. Take the rule-busting,
body:
The word disruptor is a vividly descriptive one, and it’s almost always applied to an individual. But it doesn’t have to be. Take the rule-busting, category-smashing, one-of-a-kind-because-you’ve-never-seen-anything-of-its-kind “You Can See Everything,” a movie that in one weekend has turned the movie landscape topsy-turvy.

	“You Can See Everything” is such an unprecedented cinematic wild card that as you watch it, the very question of what it is makes the movie itself a disruptor. It’s a documentary…made by a prankish cringe comedian…about a notorious white-collar criminal…that plays as a piece of hangout-movie vérité…until the actress who played the white-collar criminal in a TV series actually shows up…at which point the psychodramatic circus is just getting started.
	

	This past weekend, “You Can See Everything” made $15 million on 800 screens (complete with 2,000 sold-out shows). That made it the most successful opening for a non-music documentary since Michael Moore’s “Fahrenheit 9/11,” 22 years ago. Yet even those numbers don’t tell the story of how “You Can See Everything” has injected itself into the cultural bloodstream — and is reconfiguring the movie world. People are rushing to see it almost as a kind of mission. Audiences are alive to it; the film is so full of revelation and new-paradigm entertainment value that people often say it exceeds their expectations. This, in a word, is everything a great movie should be: an experience unlike one you’ve had before, one that lures and enthralls you, and that leaves you feeling different when it’s over.
	

	The film’s box-office numbers are likely to shoot up in its second weekend, when it expands to a full national release. And there’s every chance that the numbers could continue to go up for a week or two after that, the way they did with “Obsession.” The excitement that surrounds “You Can See Everything” rhymes with the out-of-the-box quality that drew people in hordes over the summer to see “Obsession” and “Backrooms.” This was a new kind of audience: a new demo, a new consciousness, a crystalization of the possibility that we might be on the cusp of a new “film generation.” That’s an old term (from the 1970s), one that desribed how the first generation to grow up with movies as their transcendent art form embraced them in a new way, like rock ‘n’ roll — not just as entertainment or even as art but as a fundamental expression of who they were.

	Watching “You Can See Everything,” people see themselves reflected in the post-ironic deadpan of Nathan Fielder, who is 42 and represents, from his television shows, a novel mode of fucking with people that’s intricate in its cleverness yet bizarrely honest. Having his close-up conversations with Elizabeth Holmes, he’s wily and detached, but he’s also a straight-shooter, asking rigorous questions about what we want to know: how Holmes could have lied the way she did, and, if she claims (as she does throughout the film) that she wasn’t lying, how she could possibly believe that. The movie, in a sense, is a cosmic meditation on lying. (Holmes sounds as monomaniacal, and as hard to fathom, in her systematic delusions as Donald Trump.) I think the Elizabeth Holmes showcased in “You Can See Everything” is a quintessential example of the human being as corporate performer — she’s doing a dance of put-on earnestness, and her act is so good that Fielder meets his match in attempting to unmask it. The film is an almost dreamlike duel of egos.

	By making a movie in which he and his directing partner, Lance Oppenheim, literally didn’t know where they were going, Nathan Fielder has given us a documentary drama that’s all about discovery. That’s what gives “You Can See Everything” its cathartic existential entertainment value. Like “Pulp Fiction,” it seems to be doing nothing less than reinventing what a movie can be. And the outpouring of adoration — and ticket sales — is already so undeniable that I think it’s all but certain that “You Can See Everything” will wind up being the first documentary to be nominated for best picture at the Oscars.
	

	Here’s how that would work. Right now, the film is still forging its path, but I’d wager that it has a solid shot of being named best picture by one or more of the critics’ groups (the New York Film Critics Circle, the Los Angeles Film Critics Association, the National Board of Review, and so on). That would establish its credibility as a work of cinematic art. The Oscar voters aren’t beholden to the critics, but they often follow their lead. It’s been a long time, in fact, since these two pools of tastemakers existed in any true opposition. (I know more than one critic who thinks that it’s the job of year-end critics’ voting to move the needle on the Oscars.) Voting aside, the movie is sure to top many critics’ 10 Best lists, and by the time that happens it will likely have made $100 million at the box office. Its mainstream cultural status as one of the best pictures of the year will, at that point, be undeniable. And if and when it’s nominated for best picture, that will be a ground-shifting moment.

	But here’s why I think “You Can See Everything” is also a serious contender to win. This is not an Oscar odds column, and I’m not going to try and parse the chances of “You Can See Everything” next to every film that’s been floated as a contender, from “La Bola Negra” to “Artificial” to “Project Hail Mary” to “I Play Rocky” to the yet-to-be-seen “Dune: Part Three.” But I will use “The Odyssey” as a front-running standard bearer.

	In many quarters, “The Odyssey” has acquired an aura of inevitability. It’s the big-vision version of what movies can be, and at a casual glance it connected on every level: with the critics, at the box office, as a must-see cultural phenomenon. At the same time, I think it’s a vulnerable front-runner (in a way that the last Christopher Nolan Oscar movie, “Oppenheimer,” was not), because there are a great many people who are less than in love with it.

	If “The Odyssey” wins, it will not be a surprise. It will feel very much like a traditional Oscar victory, the least disruptive one possible. But we are now in an era of disruption — and, quite strikingly, we’re in a year when disruption (from AI or wherever) isn’t just threatening the film industry. It’s looming up as one of the forces that could save it. By the time of Oscar night, “You Can See Everything” may have emerged as the year’s quintessential example of what a movie can be: an ecstatic disruption, an adventure of the spirit, one that wakes you up and startles you, that makes you want to see it again (I’m still working up the courage to go a second round with “The Odyssey”), and one that unites the audience in the feeling of having experienced something uncanny. Something we haven’t seen before. The reason I predict “You Can See Everything” will triumph at the Oscars is that anyone who votes for it won’t just be voting for best picture — they’ll be voting for the future.

schema.headline: Why ‘You Can See Everything’ Could Win Best Picture at the Oscars

title: ‘Michael’: Golden Globes Reject Submission to Compete in Comedy/Musical Categories
description:
The music of “Michael” is bringing some drama. 

	Variety has confirmed that Lionsgate’s bid to have its Michael Jackson biopic compete as a comedy
body:
The music of “Michael” is bringing some drama. 

	Variety has confirmed that Lionsgate’s bid to have its Michael Jackson biopic compete as a comedy or musical at the Golden Globes has been denied.

	The Golden Globes’ decision means the film, starring Jaafar Jackson as the King of Pop, is currently slated for the drama categories where it would compete for one of the six available slots against Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey,” Los Javis’ “La Bola Negra” and more. The supporting actor and actress categories do not separate by genre, so this has no effect on his co-stars Colman Domingo and Nia Long.
	

	Lionsgate can appeal the ruling ahead of the Oct. 31 submission deadline. If the studio moves forward, the organization’s awards committee would evaluate the appeal. According to the Golden Globes rules, it states: “A musical can be a comedy or a drama in which songs are used in addition to spoken dialogue to further the plot.”


	Under Globes procedure, when a film submits in a category that goes against the grain, or one in which it would not typically be accepted, a letter from the director is required to proceed. That letter, from “Michael” director Antoine Fuqua, was included with the studio’s submission. The organization reviewed the request and denied it anyway. An appeal may still be possible before the Oct. 31 submission deadline, but sources have shared that it will likely not be pursued. Lionsgate declined to comment.

	Musical biopics have long been tricky to classify at the Globes. “Ray” and “Walk the Line” both competed in, and won, the comedy or musical categories in the mid-2000s. Those victories prompted a rule change requiring that songs propel the narrative rather than appear as standalone performances. In other words, music alone is no longer enough to qualify a film as a musical. By that standard, “Bohemian Rhapsody,” “Elvis,” and “A Complete Unknown” were all submitted as dramas in the years since. One notable exception: “Inside Llewyn Davis,” the Coen brothers’ story of a folk singer struggling for success in 1961, was permitted to compete as a comedy during its respective year.
	

	That same distinction appears to have decided the fate of “Michael.” Jackson performs many of his uncle’s biggest hits in the film. Still, the organization evidently viewed those sequences as re-creations of Michael Jackson’s performances rather than as integral storytelling devices.

	Fuqua’s film, which opened April 24, became the first biopic in history to surpass $1 billion at the worldwide box office and is Lionsgate’s biggest release ever. It also made a star of Jaafar Jackson, who had never acted professionally before.

	The ruling does not affect the Globes’ broader slate of classification decisions. The awards show has accepted both “Obsession” and “Tender Loving Care” as comedies for consideration.

	The 84th Golden Globe nominations will be announced Monday, Dec. 7, and the ceremony, hosted by Nikki Glaser, is set for Sunday, Jan. 10.

	Gold Derby first reported this story.

title: ‘NCIS: Origins’ Producer on the Show’s Historic Mark Harmon/Michael Weatherly Reunion: ‘It Was a Special Day in My Life, Seeing That Happen After a Decade’
description: When the characters of Jethro Gibbs and Tony DiNozzo reunite for the first time in a decade in Tuesday night’s episode of “NCIS: Origins,” there wi
body:
When the characters of Jethro Gibbs and Tony DiNozzo reunite for the first time in a decade in Tuesday night’s episode of “NCIS: Origins,” there will be no head slaps — something that may disappoint a few original “NCIS” but will probably be a relief to most. After all, there’s been a lot of water under the bridge since these two characters first established a somewhat fraternal but definitely hierarchal bond when the mothership series began 23 years ago. Michael Weatherly is back on “NCIS” this season in the DiNozzo character’s new and matured role as director of the agency, while Mark Harmon‘s Gibbs remains retired but has a case of his own to solve across this entire season of the spinoff series. Their reunion at the beginning and end of the Oct. 20 “Origins” episode is short but will be extremely sweet to the fans who’ve longed to see the fictional and real men share a frame again.
	

	The hunger to see it happen was hardly lost on “NCIS: Origins” showrunner David North, who wrote for these characters on “NCIS” back in the day. The spinoff, which portrays Gibbs as an up-and-comer in the early ’90s, has intimately involved Harmon as an executive producer and narrator, but not so much an on-screen presence until a present-day flash-forward story was added for season 3. That was coup enough, in terms of bringing in some older “NCIS” fans who hadn’t yet checked out the new series, but bringing in Weatherly for a crossover moment is a cherry on top for the conjoined procedurals. 


	North talked with Variety about what this old-home week means for himself as well as franchise fans, and also addressed what we might see transpire between the young Gibbs (Austin Stowell) and his love interest, Special Agent Lala Dominguez (Mariel Molino) before the season wraps up… plus, the eternality of Ducky.
	

	For longtime “NCIS” fans, a Gibbs/DiNozzo reunion is an event. Was it something you’d hoped could happen for a long time, or does it count as much more spur of the moment than that?

	For a long time, as just a fan of the franchise, it was something I’d always hoped would happened. But to be honest, I didn’t really ever foresee it happening in “Origins,” until after season 2, when I really started coming up with this idea of a story that would happen in present-day. Once I approached Mark and pitched him a story, and he was down to do it, then we really started talking about, “OK, well, what opportunities are here and what would we want to see as fans?” Obviously getting Mark and Michael back together on set was really an ambitious idea. I’m so glad it came to fruition because it was unbelievably special to see it happen there on the day, and then we’re really proud of how it came out.

	It was awesome to see them together and to see them chatting in-between shots. And they both hit the ground running. You wouldn’t have thought there was 10 years in between. I know for all of us there, we kind of just were watching and admiring them and thinking of what they had accomplished together. It brought back a lot of memories for me, as someone who’d spent a lot of time writing the original “NCIS.”

	There is something very funny about the moment where they catch up — the “What have you been doing the last 10 years?” interchange — and DiNozzo has a lot to say, and Gibbs… does not.

	Yeah, it really was a combination of two things. Those characters, that’s just how they are. DiNozzo’s just gonna go on runs and say whatever is in his head, and Gibbs doesn’t say much. But also think about the recent years at least — DiNozzo’s gone and been doing so much, within the story [as portrayed in the “Tony and Ziva” series that aired for one season on Paramount+], so there’s room for a little recap there, and Gibbs really has been kicking back in Alaska.



	

					“Return of the Mack” — NCIS: Origins, scheduled to air Tuesday, Oct. 20 –  Pictured: Mark Harmon as Leroy Jethro Gibbs, Michael Weatherly as Tony DiNozzo. 
									CBS
	



	Obviously Michael Weatherly would not be here for a cameo if not for Mark Harmon’s wholesale return to his character. In establishing “Origins,” where originally Harmon was not on-screen for more than a few moments, was it always your intention, or at least hope, that he might show up for more of a present-day flash-forward, or did that really only come up after the series was underway?
	

	A little bit of both. You know, it’s hard when you’re producing a show and making it with Mark; of course you’re always thinking how it would be cool to see him a little bit more. But that certainly wasn’t why we got into this. Last season, we did a crossover with the original — with the mothership “NCIS” — where Mark appeared in our hour of that, and the fan response, of course, was incredible. So really it was one of those things where, after Season 2 ended, I just started thinking, “Would it be possible? Would Mark be at all interested?” In going to him and pitching him an idea, he was, and we kind of just ran from there.

	In this episode, the modern-day characters just appear at the beginning and end, in framing the ’90s storyline, which takes up most of the hour. At some point, to really develop the present-day story, you’ll probably have to devote more screen time to what the present-day Gibbs is up to. But is it fair to assume that for a lot of the season, that ratio will continue, with most of the hour set in the ’90s?

	Yeah, I mean, what we’ve seen in the first three weeks is roughly what this season is. It’s mostly our 1993 storyline, with our close-ended cases, our cool mystery of the week that we’re having a lot of fun with — some really fresh, interesting twists that we’ve come up with this year and within those cases. But then what’s happening in the serialized story in 1993 is directly informing what’s happening with Mark in present-day. And yeah, it’s been fun to be able to see Gibbs — or Mark Harmon’s Gibbs — and see how what happened in the past has come back to haunt him in the present, and things are really changing for him quickly.

	Do you think Mark ultimately has enjoyed coming back? He certainly seemed content being retired from the franchise for a while, so it was a bit of a surprise to see him coming back into the role as much as he has, and not just doing the narration.

	Certainly, I never want to speak for Mark, although I guess I’ve kind of been doing it for years, a little bit. But, yes, he’s definitely had fun, and I think he just loves this cast and crew of “Origins” so much, and the cast and crew love him. I mean, for the first two years, of course, he did his narration in a sound studio, but he popped onto set, and certainly gives feedback on scripts and things. But when I walk on the set with him, you just see the respect and the love that everyone has for him. So I think personally that was why he responded so well when he was asked to come and do this — just because he really likes these people and enjoys being around them. And so I think he’s had a lot of fun.
	

	For O.G. “NCIS” fans, the amount of young Ducky in this episode as well will be pleasing. and satisfying. What Adam Campbell brings to his interpretation of the role is a kick.

	Adam Campbell’s just phenomenal, and David McCallum, of course, who played Ducky for so many years, loved Adam and thought the world of him [when Campbell came in to “NCIS” for flashback scenes], which I think is pretty special. We always love doing young Ducky stories because they’re just so much fun. And, yeah, knowing that this would be an episode that we were putting Mark Harmon and Michael Weatherly together, I had a thought there would be some new fans that maybe weren’t watching “Origins” that were gonna tune in, and I definitely wanted to give them something that felt comfortable for them.

	You have a moment in this episode where 1990s Gibbs and Ducky make a plan to get to know each other a little better, and Harmon’s narration suggest that is a key moment in their initial bonding.

	Yeah, exactly. I mean, that friendship is, to me, one of the most legendary and epic friendships in the history of television.

	And there’s a poignant moment when present-day Gibbs sort of wishes he had reconnected with Ducky before he died, which maybe offers just a few seconds of recognizing the fact that McCallum’s not around anymore, along with establishing a character beat about how most people would feel about not having kept up with a friend who’s gone.

	Yeah. I didn’t have a lot of discussions about that with Mark. But in us writing Mark saying how much he misses him, I think that’s a really special thing for the fans, and I know Gibbs does miss Ducky just the same as Mark misses David.

	Anything to say about the young Gibbs’ love interest in this, Lala, and how that’s developing through the season?

	Yeah, we started this show as saying this was kind of the story of this great love that got away, which we’ve had a lot of fun with. And I’ll say it’s not going to be a typical procedural thing this season where you’re seeing the “will they, won’t they?” We’re going all in. Things are gonna progress fast, for better or worse.

	Of course, people wonder what the end game is, since that’s not a character referred to in the mothership show. People may be steeling themselves for tragedy or something, or at the least just wondering how you get out of this in the ultimate storyline.
	

	I’ll say I read the Reddit threads, and I haven’t had anyone predict what’s actually gonna happen yet. So that’s been cool for me. I keep thinking that at some point someone’s gonna get it. And maybe some people do, and they just don’t go to the internet and type about it. But yeah… This was a great love for Gibbs, and we get a lot of our answers this season.

	And then, of course, Gibbs fans would love to see Mark interact with every current or past cast member of “NCIS” now that he’s back on screen. You probably don’t have a lot of leeway to make it the “former ‘NCIS’ guest star of the week.” But is there a possibility for seeing more NCIS characters cross over? Or is getting Michael a big enough deal you feel you’ve fulfilled that quotient?

	No, we will. We will. [Following this interview, Emily Wickersham was announced as reprising her “NCIS” role as Ellie Bishop in several “Origins” episodes, starting Oct. 27.] Mark Harmon calls this the season of “grip it and rip it” — an old quote from John Daly, the golfer. And it has been that. So we’re not holding anything back, and we will have some special guest stars this year.



	

					“Return of the Mack” — NCIS: Origins, scheduled to air Tuesday, Oct. 20 –  Pictured: Mark Harmon as Leroy Jethro Gibbs, Michael Weatherly as Tony DiNozzo. 
									CBS
	



	For you personally, you go so far back with this franchise, but you’re not wanting to live in the past when you’re very much committed to a show that’s pretty different. But does it strike any kind of personal chord in you, or feel like exercising an old muscle or something, bringing back a character for a reunion that never seemed too likely to happen?

	Yeah. When working on that script with the writers, I commented one day, “This is crazy,” writing Gibbs and DiNozzo. The franchise means a lot to me; it’s been a big, big, huge part of my adult life, and seeing Mark and Michael together was really meaningful. It was an unbelievably incredible thing that day, and everyone there felt it. And I’m hoping that Tuesday night the fans at home will too. I think I told my dad it was a special day in my career. But really, it was a special day in my life, honestly, to see that happen after a decade.

            According to court documents, obtained by TMZ, Chloe Spence filed for a restraining order against Sahara in June 2024, alleging the model was taking unprescribed Xanax and had been in an "intoxicated delusional state" on more than one occasion.
      
    
        Waiting for your permission to load the Instagram Media.
      
    
            Spence claimed things turned physical during an April 2024 incident ... alleging Sahara charged at her, grabbed her face and dug her nails into her skin, leaving a cut and a scar beneath her left eyebrow.
      

            She also claimed Sahara made unsettling remarks that left her fearing for her safety.

            We broke the story ... Sahara died Sunday at 34, with her family telling us she was surrounded by loved ones at the hospital.
